notes: Schematic planning units: 900x720 design space; playable glass approx x=48–852, y=100–635. Rectangles are visual starting guesses only: no Unity physics validation, collision proof, measured ink budgets or 3-star pars.

sharedMechanics.description: Plate requires physical sustained contact, powers linked retracting gate while occupied; never closes on a subject; lamp/cable indicates live power.
Vertical carrier waits for pad start AND passenger; docks high and hands Pip onto prebuilt exit route; once launched finishes cycle.
Visually distinct LIFT command pad latches after valid contact; gate plate is continuous-hold.

levels.name: Push Comes to Shove
levels.question: Can you send a heavy test block to a clearly marked pressure pad so Pip's prebuilt escape rail becomes usable?
levels.novelty: First observable cause-and-effect: weight settles → lamp lights → hatch gate retracts. Pip's journey is mostly automated; the player learns the machinery.
alternatives: A modest diagonal supports the falling weight into PAD A.
A curved scoop directs the block without requiring an exact angle.
levels.player: Draw one continuous guide under the falling metal block; release and watch the pad power the gate.
levels.failure: A mark under Pip ignores the clearly labeled block; the gate remains closed and its lamp stays amber.
levels.fairness: Start with a gate occupying a visibly cut rail; PAD A, cable and gate share the same yellow circuit marking. One gate opens only while PAD A is occupied.
levels.timing: Pad latches only after stable 0.15 s of contact. Gate retracts in roughly 0.25 s. The weight should reach PAD A before Pip reaches the gate in a natural successful route.
levels.risks: Early collisions between the drawn line, installed rail and block; tune height and separate lanes. Verify block stays on PAD A without a pixel-precise stroke.
levels.hint: The steel block is the key. Give it a downhill ride to the striped plate.
levels.gate: Candidate complete when 3 loose finger-width guides activate pad and let Pip reach collector; no narrow target exploitation.
levels.implementation: NEW: one reusable weight/Pip-compatible pressure pad + sliding gate + visible lamp/wire. Reuse existing SpawnWeight, rails and pod. Never bind this level to special-case id logic.

levels.name: Door Policy
levels.tag: A tap is not a promise.
levels.question: How can a single small drawing keep a rolling crate parked on a pad long enough for Pip to cross?
levels.novelty: Switch occupancy matters. The player discovers that triggering is not the same as holding: solve by catching, not by drawing a long new route.
alternatives: Short stopper on the downhill side of the pad.
Small curved bumper that dissipates the crate's motion without bouncing it away.
levels.player: Place a short stopper beside the pad; the existing steel runway gets the crate there. When it rests, the powered gate stays open.
levels.failure: A long ramp accelerates the crate across PAD A. The light flickers and the gate closes before Pip arrives.
levels.fairness: Always show the gate lamp following actual pad occupancy; no secret activation timers or delayed reset. Visible safe closing: gate does not crush Pip and waits until clear.
levels.timing: Do not surprise-relock mid-body. If switch empties, close after a short visible grace and only when gate volume is unoccupied; contact safety is mandatory.
levels.risks: Crate center-of-mass rolling vs visually depicted contact; wide sensor collider and friction tuning required. Guard against a solution that wedges Pip on the pad.
levels.hint: The crate can reach the plate. Can it stay for the whole inspection?
levels.gate: 3 distinct short bumpers park the crate; a plain 'tap the pad' route demonstrably fails without making the gate appear arbitrary.
levels.implementation: REUSE pad and gate from 24. New behavior: continuous occupancy, anti-crush gate close interlock and visible occupied lamp. Do not use coded level-specific delay.

levels.name: Waiting Room
levels.tag: Sometimes the shortest path arrives too soon.
levels.question: The block follows an installed slow chute toward PAD A. Can you give Pip a longer, gentler route so the gate is open when he arrives?
levels.novelty: The player's single stroke changes time-of-arrival rather than opening a gate. The first deliberate 'wait by routing' puzzle in this chapter.
alternatives: A safe shallow bend that lengthens Pip's route.
A two-stage cradle that lets Pip descend after PAD A is visibly occupied.
levels.player: The weight is already guided to the plate. Draw Pip a reasonable detour before the gate, rather than racing it.
levels.failure: A short straight acceleration stroke gets Pip to the still-locked gate; he hits a visible, solid door.
levels.fairness: Weight timing should come from physics and prebuilt chute, not a hidden countdown. Failed early-arrival should produce readable 'gate locked' motion. No split-second release control.
levels.timing: Successful window must be broad (target ≥0.8 s); avoid a narrow reaction-time test or needing to pause screen interactions.
levels.risks: Fixed rail can override player route. Ensure the intended detour is physically attractive and differentiates early vs timely arrival in physics replay.
levels.hint: Pip is early. Give the block time to do the paperwork.
levels.gate: At least two meaningfully different gentle detours solve; direct short line collides closed gate; timing margin ≥0.8 s.
levels.implementation: No new mechanism. Reuse hold pad and gate; only tune trajectory and relative travel distance.

levels.name: Two Jobs, One Line
levels.question: Can one connected ink shape catch a weight onto the pad and then make Pip's landing safely clear the opened gate?
levels.novelty: The same physical drawing plays two roles on different sides: guided counterweight and Pip's escape deflector. Not merely solving two disconnected mini-puzzles.
alternatives: A descending ramp that ends in a braking shelf.
A soft hooked stroke that still presents a support to the weight and a descent for Pip.
levels.player: A single continuous shape must bring the block onto the trigger and create a safe passage for Pip.
levels.failure: A stroke that only sends the block to the pad opens the gate but drops Pip onto the wrong side of the final gap.
levels.fairness: Acknowledge any elegant creative solution with one line; do not require exact 'S' or diagram tracing. Players can see the relevant physics before release.
levels.timing: The weight must reach the pad before Pip's gate approach in viable routes; challenge is shape function, not a 0.1 s synchronized race.
levels.risks: Overly complicated geometry may become an exact-stroke contest. Reject and simplify if less than three broad gesture variants succeed.
levels.hint: Don't draw two things. Make one thing help two experiments.
levels.gate: Three flexible connected shapes independently affect both weight and Pip; short one-purpose strokes fail for understandable reasons.
levels.implementation: REUSE switch/gate and native one-stroke collision. Only a level layout; do not introduce multi-stroke or material switching.

levels.name: The Intern Goes First
levels.tag: A colleague with a temporary job.
levels.question: Can one Pip briefly hold down the pad while the other crosses a gate, then still get both into the same collector?
levels.novelty: Subjects cooperate: first arrival enables passage for second. The pad is not just an object sorter; it adds a small story with recognizable lab characters.
alternatives: A low shared nudge for the second Pip while the first passes over the switch.
A shallow deflector that lets both join after the gate.
levels.player: The intern's fixed route brings him to the switch; guide Pip through while the circuit is held. A short shared return chute carries the intern out afterward.
levels.failure: If Pip races ahead or the intern leaves the plate too soon, the light goes dark and the gate blocks him; any rescue of just one still fails.
levels.fairness: Critical feasibility rule: a switch occupant MUST have a visible physical route off the pad after the second subject safely passes. No permanently parked rescue subject. The gate stays open while a body is inside it.
levels.timing: Use broad spatial separation and physics-controlled dwell, not an invisible timer. If both cannot reach the pod on one continuous stroke, redesign before acceptance.
levels.risks: Highest risk level in batch: long dwell may trap the intern and contradict two-subject rescue. A reliable exit-from-pad route is essential, not optional.
levels.hint: The intern can hold the button. But HR insists that he gets out too.
levels.gate: Two subjects physically captured in collector, one at a time, in 3 loose stroke replays. Reject if first cannot leave plate or non-gate bypass trivializes it.
levels.implementation: Only existing Pips + plate/gate. No scripted 'intern presses button' shortcut; all triggers from real Rigidbody2D contact.

levels.name: Elevator Pitch
levels.question: Can you guide Pip aboard a clearly marked vertical lift while a fixed test block automatically powers it?
levels.novelty: First meaningful vertical travel machine. Introduce a visible lift ride, dock and short exit rail without mixing additional mechanics.
alternatives: Short entry guide to the waiting lift.
Small cradle just before the lift deck that preserves forward motion.
levels.player: The block will trigger the lift. Pip needs a reliable boarding ramp; once Pip is on the platform, the lift raises him to the exit rail.
levels.failure: A line that sends Pip past the platform leaves him below it. A correct lift clearly waits at the lower dock rather than leaving before the player can board.
levels.fairness: Lift only departs when PAD L is powered AND Pip is on its platform. Clear deck outline, docking lights and line to upper exit rail; no unexplained lift launching.
levels.timing: Travel begins automatically after visible boarding/pad conditions; moving platform smoothly carries Rigidbody2D passenger, no jump input.
levels.risks: Coupling a kinematic vertical platform with 2D collision; ensure it does not push Pip through ceilings and that upper rail catches him with broad tolerance.
levels.hint: Pip cannot reach the top. Make sure he catches his ride.
levels.gate: 3 broad entry strokes successfully board lift, ride, disembark, reach pod. No auto-capture merely from standing near lift.
levels.implementation: NEW shared vertical-lift module, reuse current carrier concept/kinematic movement, simple dock sensor. Avoid a separate cinematic or physics engine.

levels.name: Weight of Responsibility
levels.tag: The passenger is ready. The power isn't.
levels.question: Pip is already waiting on the lift. Can a compact drawn guide put a falling steel block on the plate to activate it safely?
levels.novelty: Invert 29. The player controls the machine's power sequence, not boarding; the lift is already occupied and the ink must avoid disrupting passenger.
alternatives: Compact downhill channel from the block to the plate.
Short interception plus a prebuilt fixed rail feeding PAD L.
levels.player: Pip is aboard the lift from frame one. Route the falling block into the lift circuit; use the minimal intervention to power the ride.
levels.failure: A giant stroke can strike Pip on the deck or send the weight across the empty floor instead of activating the lift.
levels.fairness: Player must see the lift occupant, its unlit circuit and the independent falling block. Do not reward drawing under Pip: he is already correctly placed.
levels.timing: The lift stays stationary until the pad is active; once started, it completes its ride even if the block bounces away (latched ride command). The PAD L appearance should communicate latched lift activation, unlike hold gates.
levels.risks: Introducing a latched motor command after hold gates may confuse players. Clearly distinguish LIFT command with up-arrow + 'READY/GO', no identical plate artwork for different semantics.
levels.hint: Pip brought himself. The motor wants a down payment.
levels.gate: Weight reaches circuit with 3 alternate finger-sized guides; elevator finishes and passenger reaches collector, no crush/no blocked upper exit.
levels.implementation: Reuse 29's lift + a one-shot motor start on sustained pad contact (not a gate occupancy rule); visually explicit latched lift state.

levels.name: Chain of Command
levels.question: Can you shape one line so a block holds the gate, and Pip uses a familiar tailwind only after the passage is open?
levels.novelty: Combines *learned* gate and existing fan in a short, observable sequence; no new trick, material or abstract control.
alternatives: A long but shallow connected stroke powers the switch then gives Pip a braking landing.
One short intercept can redirect weight and leave the installed rail doing most of Pip's trip.
levels.player: Use the line to send the block to the pad. The door opens; the air current then does the travel. Use available ink for control, not brute force.
levels.failure: A direct high-speed escape before powering the door runs into the locked shutter. A long ink bridge may keep Pip above the fan and overshoot.
levels.fairness: Open state, airflow direction and pod clearance must remain visible together; no hidden sequence flags. Only one newly learned mechanism family (gate) plus a familiar fan.
levels.timing: One clear dependency: PAD A powers door; Pip crosses then airflow nudges. Give >1 s of viable temporal slack. Unpowered gate physically blocks.
levels.risks: Too much at once if switch, gate and fan all intersect Pip draw corridor. Favor spacious board and reuse wide launch rail; reject if only microscopic line works.
levels.hint: Power first. Then let the wind file the escape paperwork.
levels.gate: Three robust broad connected drawings; one understandable failure for each omitted step; two-pip not required in finale, fatigue managed after hard 27 and 30.
levels.implementation: REUSE plate, gate, fan, rail. No lift in level 31: keeps final exam focused on two learned technologies.
